stories.title: 3 children killed in fire at water village in Sabah
stories.summary: Three children were killed in a water village fire which also destroyed hundreds of wooden and semi-permanent squatter homes in Kampong Lok Buta, near Kota Kinabalu. Firemen were called to rescue and respond to the case at around 1.40am, and reached a scene of fiery red.

stories.title: Plushies spending nights at Japan museums gain traction
stories.summary: Sending favourite stuffed animals to museums and art galleries to “spend the night” and view exhibits on their owners’ behalf is proving popular in Japan, with organisers hoping that such programmes will stir interest and attract more visitors to the facilities. The Hikone Castle Museum in Shiga Prefecture and Nagoya City Art Museum are among those who have joined a growing number of facilities hosting so-called sleepovers for plushies. The event, believed to have originated in US public libraries as a fun way to spark children’s interest in reading, is spreading across Japan, fuelled by the recent trend of people bringing their favourite plushies along with them, taking their photos and sharing them on social media. The activity is known as “nuikatsu”, a portmanteau of “nuigurumi” and “katsudo”, meaning “stuffed toys” and “activity” in Japanese. According to its officials, when the city art museum introduced the sleepover event for stuffed toys in 2025, the slots filled up instantly, only a minute after online registration opened. The Hikone Castle Museum held a similar event to commemorate its 40th anniversary,in 2027 with owners allowing their plushies to stay at the museum for a week through early August. The programme received 122 applications for just 10 available spots when applications opened in July. Hikonyan, Hikone’s mascot, served as their guide, and the stuffed animals were pictured looking at the display – swords and armour passed down through the Ii family, the feudal lords of the Hikone domain. Updates on their activity were posted regularly on social media, with a post receiving over 5,000 “likes”. Naoya Okaniwa, 47, and his wife, fans of the mascot, who travelled from Nagoya in Aichi Prefecture, central Japan, said: “We have visited the museum many times, but through these stuffed animals, we discovered charms we had overlooked.” Kanato Muraki, a seven-year-old from Kusatsu in Shiga Prefecture, who visited the facility for the first time, was impressed. “The actual armour suits were bigger than I expected.

stories.title: Over 350 police disciplinary actions overturned on appeal over 5 years
stories.summary: More than 350 disciplinary actions against police officers have been reduced, overturned or nullified over the past five years through appeals, data showed Sunday. The data, released by Rep. Park Sang-woong of the main opposition People Power Party based on figures received from the National. Police Agency, showed such cases totaled 354 from 2021 to 2025. The figures raise concerns that police disciplinary actions carry little weight, given how often the outcomes are reversed through appeal proceedings. Meanwhile, the number of appeals filed rose to 411 last year, up 34.3 percent from 2021. In some cases, officers facing dismissal appealed and kept their jobs. In one such case, an officer dismissed over a drunk driving offense was reinstated after appeal. The importance of the disciplinary system has grown, experts say, as a recent string of high-profile misconduct and negligence cases have concerned the people, including a missing woman incident on Jeju Island in which a police officer quietly dropped the investigation and closed the case. Another case involving a murder in Gwangju has drawn flak as the suspect's father, a police officer himself, is suspected of helping cover it up. Park called for stronger monitoring of police misconduct cases and tighter enforcement of discipline within the police. On the other hand, Lee Yung-hyeock, professor at Konkuk University in Seoul, suggested the frequent reversals on appeal may point to the possibility that investigations could be flawed or there was insufficient evidence against the officers involved from the outset.

stories.title: Purr-triotic ‘King Oyen’ turns heads at Malaysia’s National Day rehearsal
stories.summary: An orange cat named King Oyen stole the spotlight at Malaysia's National Day 2026 rehearsal, dressed in patriotic attire and calmly enjoying the event. King Oyen has appeared at Merdeka celebrations for four years, supported by local pet stores sponsoring his custom outfits annually. His calmness around crowds was built gradually through outdoor activities with his owner, symbolising unity and spreading national pride. Thousands gathered at Dataran Putrajaya on Aug 29 for Malaysia’s National Day 2026 full rehearsal, but an unexpected four-legged spectator stole the spotlight. Draped in a Jalur Gemilang-themed shirt, a matching tanjak, and a sleek pair of sunglasses, an orange cat named “King Oyen” proved to be a crowd favourite as spectators began arriving as early as 6.30am. Despite the loud music and massive turnout, the six-year-old feline sat unfazed beside his owner, Siti Zalifah Abdul Aziz, 53, calmly soaking in the parade. This marks the fourth consecutive year. King Oyen has joined the Merdeka festivities, following previous appearances in Kuala Lumpur and state-level celebrations in Kuantan. “He really enjoys it. He’s completely used to large crowds and cameras – in fact, he loves posing for them,” Siti said, as King Oyen looked on. She noted that local pet stores sponsor his custom patriotic outfits each year, ensuring he sports a fresh look for every celebration. Building the feline’s calm composure was a gradual process rooted in trust.
